note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hypertension and palpitations.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
49-year-old male with longstanding hypertension since young age presents for evaluation. Patient reports recent emergency room visit in March with high blood pressure and palpitations, which he attributes to consuming several cups of coffee without breakfast and describes as likely a panic attack. Has not experienced palpitations since that time. Reports family history of hypertension. Recently started on new antihypertensive regimen by new primary care physician approximately one month ago. Currently checking blood pressure at home daily in the morning, with readings consistently between 146-155 mmHg. Patient attempting to reduce salt intake and ambulating on treadmill when possible. Currently on three medications at maximum doses but blood pressure remains elevated, concerning for resistant hypertension.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies recurrent palpitations since March event.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypertension since young age.

MEDICATIONS
Benicar HCT (Olmesartan medoxomil 40 mg/Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg) - started one month ago.
Amlodipine 10 mg daily.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Significant family history of hypertension.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Drinks coffee. Attempts dietary salt restriction. Exercises by walking on treadmill when able.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Heart and lungs sound good. Abdomen soft, non-tender. No ankle or foot edema. No significant abnormalities noted.

RESULTS
Potassium one week ago: 4.0 mEq/L (normal).
Thyroid profile from March 1, 2021 - to be copied forward per physician note.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
49-year-old with resistant hypertension on three maximum-dose medications with blood pressure still not at goal. Likely secondary hypertension given early onset and inadequate response to maximal therapy. Discussed possible hormonal etiology including hyperaldosteronism. Adding spironolactone to current antihypertensive regimen. Counseled on side effects including dizziness, electrolyte disturbances (hyperkalemia, hyponatremia), dehydration, and rare gynecomastia (1 in 100 males). Advised need for adequate hydration. Instructed on DASH diet and salt restriction to <2000 mg/day (ideally 1500 mg/day). Encouraged regular aerobic exercise for 30 minutes most days. Provided heart.org website for additional education. Metabolic panel and blood pressure check scheduled in two weeks to monitor potassium and sodium levels. If inadequate control on spironolactone, next option is carvedilol followed by referral to resistant hypertension clinic for evaluation of secondary causes and consideration of procedure-based interventions such as renal denervation. Follow-up appointment in two weeks.
